reason: I expected to break this one and could not, but the attack was worth running and it changes what the editor should believe about the evidence. THE ATTACK. This line has a live comma variant. The brief's own Calendar For Life candidate (cflId 1, JANUARY-1) prints "Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry, and narrow-mindedness", with a serial comma after bigotry, and so do Goodreads, the quotation sites and most secondary printings. The verifier ships it WITHOUT that comma. One of the two is drift, and the verifier's only witness was Gutenberg 3176, whose header, I checked, carries no "Original publication" statement at all: it is a David Widger transcription, most recently updated September 2025, with no stated copy-text. So the evidence field's claim to "the 1869 American Publishing Company edition" was, on the verifier's own showing, asserted rather than shown, and if the 1869 setting had the serial comma the shipped line would be wrong in the very edition it names. THE RESULT. I went to the 1869 setting itself. Two independent Internet Archive scans of the American Publishing Company edition, innocentsabroad00twairich and innocentsabroad07twaigoog, both print the sentence on page 650, under the running head CONCLUSION, and both read: Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts. No serial comma, in either scan, with the line break falling inside "bigot-ry" in both. The same setting elsewhere reads "Ignorance, Bigotry and" without a serial comma too, so this is the compositor's consistent style and not a one-off. Quote Investigator independently places the sentence at page 650 of the 1869 American Publishing Company printing in the same wording. The verifier's line is therefore right and the popular version, including the Calendar For Life text this card is meant to replace, is the drifted one. That is worth saying loudly, because the natural instinct at selection will be to "fix" the card to match the app, and that would introduce the error. Locator: correct. The CONCLUSION heading sits at line 18641 of Gutenberg 3176 and the sentence at 18703, in the paragraph that begins "I have no fault to find with the manner in which our excursion was conducted", exactly as claimed, and the 1869 scans agree. Gates: shipped.js returns shipped [] and near [], normalises Twain to samuel clemens, gives 0 for the year, cap 3, not banned. No Twain in the carry-ins and no second Twain among June's proposals, so this is the cleanest of the four on collisions. In scope: 1869, not scripture, film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory, nothing needing a content warning. Source line is 50 characters, leads with the author's name, no dash. Tag Essay: The Innocents Abroad is a travel book assembled out of newspaper letters, which is nobody's idea of an essay, but the closed vocabulary offers no travel or memoir tag and Essay is where the house has put comparable prose before, including carry-in 02-cfl-03 for Stevenson's The Silverado Squatters. Correct within the vocabulary available. Theme: the line is about prejudice being burned off by seeing, which is the clear-eye half of June. ONE REMARK. I am offering a betterCitation not because the shipped one is wrong but because it is now provably stronger: the page is verified in two scans of the named edition, so the source line can carry p. 650 and the publisher, which turns the weakest evidence of the four into the best. It is 88 characters and breaks no rule. If the editor prefers the shorter line, the existing one still ships honestly; but the evidence field should be rewritten either way, since its claim about the 1869 edition was true by luck rather than by checking, and it should now cite the scans rather than the Gutenberg header.
betterCitation: Mark Twain, The Innocents Abroad, Conclusion, p. 650 (American Publishing Company, 1869)
